results.key_finding: Painful tonic spasms occur in approximately 11% of MS patients and result from ectopic axonal firing from demyelinated corticospinal or corticobulbar tracts. They are stereotyped, brief (30-120 seconds), often provoked by movement or sensory stimuli, and respond to carbamazepine or gabapentin.
results.title: Painful tonic spasms in CNS demyelinating disease: clinical features and pathophysiology

results.key_finding: Paroxysmal symptoms — including tonic spasms, trigeminal neuralgia, Lhermitte sign, and paroxysmal dysarthria-ataxia — are characteristic of MS and arise from demyelinated plaques generating ectopic impulse activity. Recognition is important to avoid misdiagnosis as focal seizures.
results.title: Paroxysmal symptoms in CNS demyelinating disorders: pathophysiology and management

results.key_finding: Multiple sclerosis with onset after age 40 years (late-onset MS, LOMS) represents 9.4-12% of all MS cases. LOMS patients more frequently have progressive features from onset, greater MRI lesion burden at diagnosis, and broader differential diagnoses including cerebrovascular disease, malignancy, and metabolic conditions. DMT efficacy appears preserved in LOMS.

output.summary: Painful tonic spasms are a recognized paroxysmal symptom of MS caused by ectopic axonal firing from demyelinated plaques in the corticospinal tracts. They are brief, stereotyped, and often triggered by movement or sensory stimuli, and may be mistaken for focal epileptic seizures. Late-onset MS (after age 40) accounts for approximately 10% of cases, presents diagnostic challenges due to broader differentials including cerebrovascular disease, and typically has greater MRI lesion burden at diagnosis. Disease-modifying therapies should be offered based on disease activity.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not diagnose MS based on lesions alone without applying the 2024 revised McDonald criteria and excluding neurosarcoidosis, NMOSD, and SLE-related CNS disease

Do not order EEG to evaluate painful tonic spasms in this context — they are a recognized paroxysmal MS symptom, not focal seizures; misclassification as epilepsy leads to harmful antiepileptic drug prescribing without disease-modifying benefit
Do not start natalizumab without first determining JC virus antibody serostatus — PML risk in JCV-antibody-positive patients is unacceptable without informed consent and risk stratification
Do not initiate fingolimod without a baseline ECG and first-dose bradyarrhythmia monitoring; avoid in patients with significant cardiac conduction disease
Do not use chronic oral corticosteroids as maintenance therapy for MS — ineffective long-term and carry serious metabolic and bone density harms

Do not attribute the hypercalcemia to the MS diagnosis — mild PTH-independent hypercalcemia warrants further workup (e.g., 1,25-OH vitamin D, chest imaging) to exclude occult granulomatous disease even after MS is confirmed
required_recommendations: Establish dissemination in space (DIS) using brain MRI in ≥2 MS-typical regions (periventricular, juxtacortical/cortical, infratentorial, spinal cord) plus extend imaging to spinal cord
Establish dissemination in time (DIT) — in this case satisfied by simultaneous enhancing and non-enhancing lesions on the brain MRI; additionally confirmed by CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands

Exclude neurosarcoidosis: order serum ACE, CSF ACE, and calcium with PTH; normal ACE in serum and CSF with PTH-independent hypercalcemia reduces but does not eliminate neurosarcoidosis risk — no leptomeningeal enhancement further argues against it
Exclude NMOSD and MOGAD with AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG cell-based assays before committing to an MS diagnosis and DMT
Recognize painful tonic spasms as a paroxysmal MS symptom (ectopic corticospinal axonal firing), NOT epileptic seizures — carbamazepine or gabapentin for symptomatic relief; EEG NOT required
Treat the acute relapse with high-dose IV methylprednisolone (1 g daily for 3-5 days)

Initiate a disease-modifying therapy after relapse stabilization; check JC virus antibody serostatus before considering natalizumab; given disease activity (multiple lesions, enhancing lesion), high-efficacy DMT is appropriate
Recognize prior episodes of right-sided visual loss with periorbital pain as misdiagnosed optic neuritis (not migraine aura) — confirmed by right RNFL thinning on OCT and prolonged VEP P100 latency

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG has no role in MS diagnosis. The painful tonic spasms are a recognized paroxysmal MS symptom, not epileptic seizures — EEG would be non-diagnostic and misleading.
CT is markedly inferior to MRI for visualising demyelinating plaques; adds radiation without diagnostic benefit in confirmed MS workup.
No cardiac indication in this MS workup; echocardiography does not inform the demyelinating differential in this patient.
Cardiac monitoring is only indicated for first-dose fingolimod (bradyarrhythmia risk) — not part of MS diagnostic evaluation.
FDG-PET is not indicated for MS diagnosis; does not differentiate demyelination from neurosarcoidosis or other mimics and adds substantial cost.

key_clinical_evidence: the 2024 revised McDonald criteria require DIS and DIT plus exclusion of a better explanation — simultaneous enhancing (left corona radiata) and non-enhancing lesions on the same brain MRI satisfies DIT on a single scan without requiring follow-up imaging

Late-onset MS (onset after age 40) accounts for approximately 10% of MS cases and presents with broader differentials including cerebrovascular disease, neurosarcoidosis, and malignancy; it should not be dismissed as 'too old for MS'

Painful tonic spasms are a pathognomonic paroxysmal MS symptom arising from ectopic corticospinal axonal discharge in demyelinated plaques; they are not epileptic seizures and respond to carbamazepine, not antiepileptic polytherapy

Prior episodes of unilateral visual loss with periorbital pain, each lasting 2-3 weeks and resolving spontaneously, are virtually diagnostic of optic neuritis — retrospective identification as prior attacks is critical for counting disease duration and DMT urgency

Mild PTH-independent hypercalcemia raises neurosarcoidosis (which can produce leptomeningeal enhancement and cranial neuropathies); the combination of normal serum/CSF ACE, no leptomeningeal enhancement, and typical MS lesion distribution argues strongly against sarcoidosis, but cannot be dismissed without these data

Low-titer ANA (1:40, speckled) is present in approximately 5-10% of healthy individuals and in many non-lupus autoimmune conditions; with negative dsDNA and Sm antibodies and no systemic SLE features, this does not constitute CNS lupus and should not derail the MS workup

AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG must be ordered as cell-based assays; short-segment, peripherally located cord lesions in this case are typical for MS and inconsistent with the longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis of NMOSD

OCT RNFL and GCL thinning in the right eye objectively confirms prior right optic nerve axonal loss from recurrent optic neuritis, reclassifying those events from 'migraine aura' to confirmed prior MS attacks

Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: McDonald 2024: dissemination in space and time is established on MRI, and oligoclonal bands substitute for dissemination in time rather than being required — the reviewers' point.

July 2026 review applied end to end: brain and cervical/thoracic cord MRI use an MS protocol; CSF is conditional, never mandatory; OCT/VEP and AQP4/MOG testing answer selected optic or atypical questions rather than forming a blanket panel.

The 2024 revised McDonald framework recognizes the optic nerve as a fifth topography and accepts the kappa free-light-chain index as an alternative positive-CSF marker; these additions do not make optic testing or lumbar puncture universal.

patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. Carvalho is a 46-year-old right-handed Afro-Brazilian secondary school teacher who presents to the neurology service for evaluation of a three-week history of progressive right-sided leg weakness, numbness below the waist, and stereotyped painful muscle contractions in the right arm and leg. Her symptoms began approximately three weeks ago with a tingling, electric sensation in both feet that initially she attributed to prolonged standing at work. Over the following week, she developed right leg weakness that made stair climbing difficult, accompanied by a band-like tightness around her lower chest. She noted that her bladder urgency has worsened over this period, with two near-incontinence episodes. She denies frank urinary retention.

The most distressing symptom has been episodic, intensely painful stiffening of the right arm and leg occurring 4-6 times daily, each lasting 30-90 seconds. These episodes are stereotyped — the right arm flexes at the elbow and the right leg extends — and are sometimes triggered by touching the right arm or by sudden movement. She has no loss of consciousness, no tongue biting, and no postictal confusion during these events. Her husband observed three episodes and confirms they are focal, brief, and do not spread to involve the face or cause loss of awareness.

Four years ago, she experienced two episodes of transient visual blurring in her right eye, each lasting 2-3 weeks, accompanied by mild aching pain behind the right eye. These were attributed to 'atypical migraine with visual aura' by a general neurologist; no MRI brain was obtained at the time, and her vision recovered fully on both occasions. She did not pursue further workup. In retrospect, both episodes likely represented right-sided optic neuritis.

Six months ago, routine blood work revealed mild hypercalcemia (10.6 mg/dL). PTH was checked and was normal. The cause of the hypercalcemia was not pursued further as the patient was lost to follow-up. She has been on amlodipine for hypertension for three years with good blood pressure control. She is a former smoker (5 pack-years, quit 10 years ago) and has no occupational or environmental exposures to dust, birds, or mold.

The patient denies fevers, weight loss, night sweats, rash, joint swelling, oral ulcers, or lymphadenopathy. She has no prior neurological hospitalizations. Family history is negative for MS or demyelinating disease.

She describes these as intensely painful, involuntary stiffening episodes that are stereotyped in character. EDSS estimated at 3.5.
